summary: Visitors from most of Europe, North America, Oceania, East Asia and the Gulf can obtain a 30-day visa on arrival (about US$51) at Dhaka and other international airports, while other nationalities — including Indian citizens — must arrange a visa through a Bangladeshi mission or the official online portal before traveling.

Satellite phones require prior authorization and are seized at the border without it.

payments.text: Cards work at upmarket hotels, restaurants and malls in Dhaka and Chattogram, but Bangladesh runs on cash and mobile money (bKash). Carry taka for markets, rickshaws and everything outside the big cities.

safety.text: Most visits are trouble-free, but petty crime in Dhaka, chaotic road travel and periodic political demonstrations — which can turn violent and shut down transport — call for caution. Avoid all protests, and note that foreigners need prior permission for the Chittagong Hill Tracts.

bestTimeToVisit.text: November to February is dry and relatively cool — the best window for Dhaka, the Sundarbans and Cox's Bazar. The monsoon (roughly June–October) brings heavy rain and flooding, with cyclone risk in the Bay of Bengal either side of it.

tips.text: For the visa on arrival, carry the fee (about US$51) in exact US dollar cash, plus printed hotel bookings and your return ticket. The counter takes no cards and officers ask for supporting documents.

Political demonstrations and hartals (general strikes) can erupt with little notice, turn violent and paralyze transport. Avoid all rallies and processions, and build slack into travel plans around election periods and political anniversaries.

The June–October monsoon regularly floods roads and delays flights, and cyclones can strike coastal areas (including Cox's Bazar) in April–May and October–November — monitor forecasts in those windows.
Foreigners need prior permission from the authorities to visit the Chittagong Hill Tracts (Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Bandarban) — arrange it well ahead through a tour operator, and expect checkpoints.
Dress conservatively, especially outside Dhaka's affluent districts, and during Ramadan eat, drink and smoke discreetly in public during daylight hours.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Bangladesh?
faq.answer: Almost everyone needs one, but many tourists get it at the airport: citizens of most European countries, the US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, China, Russia and the Gulf states can obtain a 30-day visa on arrival for about US$51. Other nationalities apply through a Bangladeshi mission, starting online at visa.gov.bd. A short list of countries — mostly Commonwealth small states — is visa-free.

faq.question: How does Bangladesh's visa on arrival work?
faq.answer: Eligible tourists pay about US$51 in cash at Dhaka (or another international airport) for a single-entry, 30-day stay. Bring a return ticket, hotel details and roughly US$500 in funds or a card statement — issuance is at the officer's discretion, so confirm eligibility with your airline before flying.

faq.question: Can I extend my stay in Bangladesh?
faq.answer: Yes — visa extensions are handled by the Department of Immigration and Passports in Dhaka (Agargaon). Apply before your current stay expires; tourist stays are typically extended by up to 30 days at a time.

faq.question: Do Indian citizens need a visa for Bangladesh?
faq.answer: Yes — Indian passport holders are not eligible for the visa on arrival and must obtain a visa in advance from a Bangladeshi mission in India. Apply well before travel, as processing times and requirements change.

faq.question: Is Bangladesh safe to visit?
faq.answer: Most trips are trouble-free, and Bangladeshis are famously hospitable. The realistic risks are road accidents, petty crime in crowded areas and political unrest. Avoid demonstrations, use reputable transport, and check your government's latest advice before you go.
